description: I am a Computer Science and Engineering student with a strong interest in Machine Learning, Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, and Space Technology. I enjoy solving real-world problems through technology, working on innovative projects, and learning new skills. I am excited to participate in NASA Space Apps Challenge to collaborate, innovate, and turn creative ideas into impactful solutions.
summary:
We built the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser, an interactive web app that turns NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) data into a landing-site navigator for the Moon. It covers 15 CLPS deliveries, 50 payloads, and 9,087 IAU-named lunar features from the USGS Gazetteer.

The core is the Sun & Earth Site Navigator: for any site and date, it computes the Sun's and Earth's elevation and azimuth, sunlight and Earth-visibility hours over 7, 14, or 29.5-day windows, and the next sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, and Earthset — the exact factors that decide whether a lander has power and can communicate. A comparison view ranks sites by power and communications, and a dedicated South Pole page covers the 14 Artemis III candidate regions, honestly flagging that only 3 have verified coordinates.

This matters because CLPS data is scattered across mission pages and catalogs, while landing-site choice hinges on illumination and visibility. Our browser makes that analysis visual, verifiable, and open to students, researchers, and space enthusiasts — not just mission planners.
details:
What it does

The CLPS Lunar Mission Browser is a free, open web app that brings NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) data and lunar landing-site analysis together in one place. It covers 15 CLPS deliveries, 50 payloads from 6 providers, and 9,087 IAU-named lunar features from the USGS Gazetteer.

Its core is the Sun & Earth Site Navigator. Choose any landing site and any date and time, and the app computes the Sun's and Earth's elevation and azimuth, sunlight and Earth-visibility hours over 7, 14, or 29.5-day windows, and the next sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, and Earthset. A time slider with play and pause animates the Sun and Earth across the sky, and a 3D scene lights the Moon from the true Sun direction. A comparison view ranks sites by power (sunlight) and communications (Earth visibility), and a dedicated South Pole page covers the 14 Artemis III candidate regions. The Lunar Feature Explorer plots all 9,087 Gazetteer features on a 3D globe and a flat map, with density heat maps and filters by type, size, and location. A science library explains the Moon behind the data: the water-ice discovery timeline, landing hazards, the lunar interior, and composition — every claim linked to its source.

How it works

The physics is a purpose-built, pure-TypeScript engine on top of the astronomy-engine library: the sub-Earth point from lunar libration, the sub-solar point from Meeus' Astronomical Algorithms (chapter 53), and event-finding by scan and bisection to about one-minute precision. It is validated against Meeus Example 53.a and Apollo 11 landing geometry, and positions are good to about ±0.3°. The app assumes an ideal geometric horizon — terrain is not modelled — and says so wherever it matters. All state lives in the URL, so any view is a shareable link. The site is a static web app, so it loads fast and runs entirely in the browser.

Benefits

CLPS mission data is scattered across NASA pages, provider sites, and catalogs, and landing-site choice hinges on two things: sunlight for power and Earth visibility for communication. This browser puts the data and that analysis in one place, in minutes instead of hours of manual lookup. Every record cites its source, and anything unverified is shown as unknown rather than guessed — for example, only 3 of the 14 south-pole candidate regions have published coordinates, and the app flags the other 11 instead of inventing positions. It is free, needs no install, and works on any device with a browser.

Intended impact

We want students, researchers, and space enthusiasts to explore lunar missions the way mission planners do — by asking "what is the Sun doing here, on this date?" instead of reading a static table. By making illumination and visibility analysis visual and verifiable, the project supports CLPS and Artemis-era thinking about where to land, and shows that honest, source-cited data can be a feature in itself. The code is open source (MIT), so other teams can reuse the Sun/Earth engine and the Gazetteer dataset for their own tools.

Tools and technology

TypeScript, React 18, Vite, and Tailwind CSS; Three.js for the 3D scenes, Leaflet for the maps, Recharts for the charts, and the astronomy-engine library for the celestial mechanics. The dataset pipeline is plain Node.js, and quality is guarded by 197 automated Vitest tests plus typechecking and linting. The site is hosted on Vercel and the code is on GitHub. No hardware was used — it is a pure software web application.

How it is creative

Most mission browsers are catalogs. Ours is a time machine: it simulates the Sun and Earth over any date, turning a static list of landing sites into a living question of light and contact. The 3D globe of 9,087 features makes the whole Moon explorable at a glance, and the honest-data approach — showing gaps instead of hiding them — turns a limitation into a design principle.

Factors the team considered

Power and communications first, because they decide whether a lander survives and can phone home. Data accuracy above completeness: verified sources only, unknown means unknown. The south pole first, because that is where Artemis III is headed. Usability: shareable links, keyboard-operable lists, and reduced-motion support. And performance: lazy-loaded 3D and charts, and 3D models compressed from 7.62 MB to 1.40 MB, so the site stays fast on real-world connections.
